alice (customer): Hey team — we hit a bunch of 429s this morning on our Dedicated pool during a batch job spike. SLA says 1k qps reserved but our job sent short bursts of 5k qps for ~40s and we saw errors and elevated latency. Can you help explain what's happening and what to tune?

maria (support): Sorry you're seeing this — can you paste the pool id, model, region, and an example request id? Also did responses stream or return as a single payload?

alice (customer): pool-id: rp-9043-eu, model: gptx-variant-2, region: eu-west-1, request_id: r-20260301-33a. Responses are single response (not streaming). It was a scheduled batch run (internal analytics) that spikes every 12h. We expected Dedicated to absorb short bursts — docs mention burst headroom?

kevin (eng-sre): quick read: Dedicated pools use token-bucket style gating per-reserved-pool + per-route enforcement. Reserved commit = sustained throughput; burst headroom is limited and depends on current token balance across the pool. If you exceed both pool burst and per-client ceilings you'll see 429s. Can you share client-side pattern (concurrency, avg tokens per request)?

alice (customer): our job opens 200 concurrent connections, each sends 25 short requests/sec for ~40s -> ~5000 rps. Each request ~140 tokens avg. We expected autofallback to hosted or queued bursts?

jun (eng-runtime): thanks, that pattern explains it. Two things likely at play: 1) reserved pool sustained qps is enforced as a long-window average; 2) burst capacity is tracked by a short refill window — if a previous sustained workload already drained headroom, a sudden spike will run out of tokens and trigger 429s. Additionally, non-streaming responses can increase per-request accounting because we bill/measure final token counts at completion which affects concurrent token allocation.

kevin (eng-sre): diagnostic check you can run on your side: tail the response headers from a failing request. We attach rate headers like:

```
X-RateLimit-Pool: rp-9043-eu
X-RateLimit-Limit: 1000
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0
X-RateLimit-Reset: 21
X-RateLimit-Burst-Window: 60
```

If Remaining is 0 and Reset is small you'll see immediate 429s. Also check our metrics: `reserved_pool.tokens.available`, `reserved_pool.burst.tokens_used`, and `route.request.denied.429`. I can pull those if you want.

alice (customer): got a sample header from one failed request, matches the Remaining:0 case. Yes please pull the metrics, would help our postmortem.

ops-bot: incident created: #INC-2026-031-45 (assigned to eng-sre)

kevin (eng-sre): pulled metrics for rp-9043-eu over the 2h window. Observations: sustained baseline ~900 qps, token balance was low due to prior hourly jobs; at spike time burst tokens dropped to near-zero within 15s and denial rate spiked. No backend OOMs or infra scaling events. Outcome = token exhaustion at pool-level.

jun (eng-runtime): repro checklist for you to run in a staging pool:
1) run a sustained load at near-commit (950 qps) for 5m to simulate drained headroom
2) inject a short high-rate spike (5k qps for 40s) from multiple hosts
3) observe `X-RateLimit-Remaining` and `reserved_pool.burst.tokens_used` during spike
4) compare streaming vs non-streaming (streaming holds fewer concurrent token allocations in some models)

Sample repro script (bash)::
```
#!/bin/bash
# simple artillery-style loop, replace TOKEN and ENDPOINT
TOKEN=REDACTED
ENDPOINT=https://inference.redwood.example/v1/generate
for i in {1..200}; do
  (while true; do
    curl -s -X POST "$ENDPOINT" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -d '{"model":"gptx-variant-2","input":"short prompt","max_tokens":140}' &
    sleep 0.05
  done) &
done
wait
```
Note: adjust concurrency and sleep to shape the spike. Watch headers.

maria (support): mitigation options while we coordinate:
- Schedule batch spread (stagger concurrent workers) to avoid single 40s spike
- Enable burst-reserve on your Dedicated contract (adds per-minute buffer) if you expect regular spikes
- Route heavy non-latency-critical jobs to a separate Dedicated pool or Hosted fallback with rate-priority rules
- For immediate relief, reduce concurrency or increase inter-request sleep to keep effective qps < pool limit + burst headroom

alice (customer): Are there billing or SLA implications if we request extra burst allowance? We're on annual reserved capacity.

maria (support): extra burst reserve is billed as an add-on (agreed in contract) — we can do a temporary uplift for emergencies. SLA remains the same for reserved capacity but measured against the new buffer level if you purchase burst add-on. I'll open a commercial ticket.

kevin (eng-sre): long-term we recommend one of: (A) increase committed qps for that pool, (B) create a second dedicated pool for cron/batch with its own commit, or (C) rework client to do gradual ramp (token bucket smoothing) so bursts are absorbed. Also consider enabling per-route smoothing rules in Console: `burst_smoothing: {window: 60s, max_burst: 2000}`.

jun (eng-runtime): FYI for engineering: we should add a clearer metric in Console for "burst headroom seconds" and a webhook alert when pool token balance falls under 10% for >30s. Filing a runtime enhancement.

maria (support): next steps: I'll attach the metrics and ops runbook to INC-2026-031-45 and start a billing uplift thread. Kevin/jun can you validate the repro steps and share any quick autoscaling tweaks we can apply to reduce risk?

kevin (eng-sre): validating repro now on staging cluster rp-stg-12, will report back in ~30m.

jun (eng-runtime): ack, will test streaming vs non-streaming accounting differences and post results.

alice (customer): thanks everyone — we'll also try spreading the cron and will update this thread after we test the repro. :heart:

maria (support): closing loop here once we have the staging repro artifacts and a billing path. Feel free to ping me directly if you need a quick emergency uplift. :thumbsup:
